reference.source: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
clinicalPearls: Haemorrhoidal thrombosis is acute clotting within haemorrhoidal tissue, ranging from an isolated thrombosed external haemorrhoid to an acute crisis of thrombosed, prolapsed, and oedematous internal or mixed haemorrhoids
The hallmark is sudden severe anal pain with a tense, tender, blue-purple swelling; extensive prolapsed thrombosis produces a circumferential oedematous painful mass at the anal verge
It is often precipitated by straining, constipation, diarrhoea, pregnancy, or childbirth
Acutely incarcerated, thrombosed, prolapsed internal haemorrhoids may become irreducible and, rarely, progress to ulceration, necrosis, or sepsis
Diagnosis is clinical on inspection; painful examination and instrumentation should be deferred or done under anaesthesia in severe cases
Most cases settle with conservative care: analgesia, stool softening, warm baths, topical agents, and reduction of oedema, with full assessment once the acute episode resolves
Early surgery (excisional haemorrhoidectomy) can be offered for severe or extensive acute thrombosis in suitable patients and gives durable results, but carries risks in the oedematous acute setting
The differential includes strangulated rectal prolapse, perianal abscess, and, in immunocompromised patients, a threshold for concern about necrosis and sepsis
reference.pathophysiology: Haemorrhoidal thrombosis develops when blood within the dilated vessels of the haemorrhoidal cushions clots, either from venous stasis and raised pressure or from an acute rise in intra-abdominal and anal pressure that ruptures or occludes vessels. In external thrombosis a discrete clot forms in the subcutaneous plexus below the dentate line. In an acute internal or mixed haemorrhoidal crisis, prolapsed cushions become trapped by sphincter spasm, which impairs venous return, causing progressive engorgement, thrombosis, and marked oedema; the swelling worsens the incarceration in a self-perpetuating cycle. The tense, clotted, oedematous tissue stretches somatically innervated anoderm, producing intense pain, and in severe incarceration the compromised blood supply may lead to mucosal ulceration, necrosis, and, rarely, secondary infection.
additionalDifferentials: Crohn disease with acute perianal inflammation
Pigmented perianal lesion such as melanoma
additionalInvestigations: Inspection and gentle digital examination to confirm thrombosed haemorrhoidal tissue
Examination under anaesthesia when pain precludes assessment or surgery is planned
Proctoscopy once the acute episode settles, to grade residual haemorrhoids
Full blood count if bleeding is significant or infection is suspected
Assessment for constipation, diarrhoea, or pregnancy as precipitants
Histology of excised tissue where appearances are atypical
redFlags: Necrosis, ulceration, or spreading infection of the thrombosed mass
Systemic sepsis, particularly in immunocompromised or diabetic patients
Irreducible incarcerated prolapse with compromised viability
A pigmented or indurated lesion suggesting malignancy
reference.prognosis: Most haemorrhoidal thromboses are self-limiting, with pain settling over days to a couple of weeks under conservative care; early excisional surgery in appropriate patients relieves symptoms quickly and reduces recurrence, while severe incarcerated thrombosis with necrosis is uncommon but carries greater morbidity.
pitfalls: Confusing incarcerated thrombosed haemorrhoids with strangulated rectal prolapse or abscess
Aggressive instrumentation of an acutely painful anus without anaesthesia
Simple incision of a clot rather than excision, leading to recurrence and residual tag
Underestimating necrosis or sepsis in immunocompromised patients
Neglecting to correct constipation, straining, or diarrhoea, allowing recurrence
references: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
Association of Coloproctology of Great Britain and Ireland guidance on haemorrhoidal disease
Standard coloproctology reference texts on acute anorectal emergencies
management: Conservative first-line care with oral analgesia, stool softeners and bulking agents, warm sitz baths and increased dietary fibre and fluids
Topical glyceryl trinitrate or a topical calcium channel blocker to relieve sphincter spasm, with topical anaesthetic or corticosteroid preparations for symptom relief
Early excision of an isolated thrombosed external haemorrhoid within the first few days for rapid and durable pain relief
Urgent haemorrhoidectomy or examination under anaesthesia for an acutely incarcerated, thrombosed and prolapsed crisis
Monitor for progression to ulceration, necrosis or sepsis in severe incarcerated disease
Deferred proctoscopy once the acute episode settles to grade residual haemorrhoids and plan definitive treatment
Address precipitants such as constipation, diarrhoea, straining and pregnancy-related factors
